claim: Without external feedback, LLM self-correction on reasoning tasks fails and can lower accuracy.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback.
authors: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou
title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
transfer: Run revise steps only when a real check output exists (tests, rule check). Skip self-revision on pure-opinion items.

claim: A critical survey found no prior work showing successful self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback alone, except on unusually suitable tasks; it works with reliable external feedback or after large-scale fine-tuning. Many positive studies had unfair setups.
authors: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang
title: When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
transfer: Treat any self-critique gain claimed without external feedback or equal-token control as unproven. Use the survey checklist when testing our own revise step.

claim: LLMs are not reliably better at discriminating among their own earlier answers than at generating a first answer, so judge-your-own-answers loops cannot be assumed to help.
quote: models are not reliably better at discriminating among previously-generated alternatives than generating initial responses.
authors: Jiang, Zhang, Weller, Weir, Van Durme, Khashabi
title: SELF-[IN]CORRECT: LLMs Struggle with Discriminating Self-Generated Responses
transfer: Do not let the same model pick the best of its own candidates by opinion. Prefer a program check or majority across independent calls.

claim: Failed self-correction is mainly a failure to find the mistake, not to fix it: given the error location, correction improved results on five reasoning tasks.
authors: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen, Mak
title: LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
transfer: Put effort into locating the failing step with a real signal (execution, rule check); then revise only that step.

claim: Chain-of-thought prompting reduced performance on three of six tasks chosen because deliberation makes humans worse; the largest drop was 36.3 points for o1-preview versus GPT-4o.
authors: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths
title: Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse
transfer: Tag task types where deliberation hurts (implicit learning, verbal-overshadowing style tasks) and route them to the bare first answer.

claim: Prompting reasoning models to keep thinking first helps, then hurts; the gain may be an artifact of added output variance meeting the metric. Parallel independent paths with majority vote gave up to 20% higher accuracy than extended thinking at the same budget (authors' claim).
authors: Ghosal, Chakraborty, Reddy, Lu, Wang, Manocha, Huang, Ghavamzadeh, Bedi
title: Does Thinking More always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
transfer: Cap serial re-thinking rounds; spend the budget on independent attempts plus a vote. Stop rule: stop when extra thinking stops changing the answer.

claim: Longer reasoning lowers accuracy on built tasks (counting with distractors, spurious-feature regression, constraint-tracking deduction); failure modes differ by model family (Claude distracted by irrelevant info, o-series overfit to framing).
authors: Gema, Hagele, Chen, Arditi, et al.
title: Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute
transfer: Do not scale thinking length blindly on tasks with distractors; strip irrelevant context before long reasoning and test several budgets.

claim: At equal inference compute, standard models beat reasoning models on low-complexity puzzles, reasoning models win at medium complexity, and both collapse at high complexity. Reasoning effort also declines past a complexity point even with budget left.
quote: low-complexity tasks where standard models outperform LRMs
authors: Shojaee, Mirzadeh, Alizadeh, Horton, Bengio, Farajtabar
title: The Illusion of Thinking
transfer: Matches our data (plain beats scaffold on easy single-answer items). Route by difficulty estimate: bare on easy, scaffold on medium, accept failure or decompose on hard. Note: I did not check published critiques of the setup.

claim: Reasoning models overthink simple problems, spending large compute for little gain; the authors propose self-training to shorten reasoning without losing accuracy on GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME.
authors: Chen, Xu, Liang, He, et al.
title: Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
transfer: Early-stop rule: once a first answer is reached and a cheap check passes, do not open more reasoning rounds.

claim: Reasoning models are poorly calibrated on very easy problems (DUMB500 set); a training-free decoding method improves calibration of token spend.
authors: Pu, Saxon, Hua, Wang
title: ThoughtTerminator: Benchmarking, Calibrating, and Mitigating Overthinking in Reasoning Models
transfer: Set a token cap from outside by estimated difficulty; remind the model of the remaining budget.

claim: In agentic software tasks (4,018 SWE-Bench Verified trajectories), higher overthinking (analysis paralysis, rogue actions, premature disengagement) correlated with lower success; picking the candidate with the lower overthinking score raised performance by almost 30% and cut cost 43% (authors' claim).
quote: favor extended internal reasoning chains over environmental interaction
authors: Cuadron, Li, Ma, Wang, et al.
title: The Danger of Overthinking: Examining the Reasoning-Action Dilemma in Agentic Tasks
transfer: Impasse detector: if the agent plans for long without acting on the environment, force an action or a tool check.

claim: CoT explanations can be unfaithful: biasing features (e.g. answer always A) change answers and accuracy drops by up to 36% on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks, while the explanation does not mention the bias.
authors: Turpin, Michael, Perez, Bowman
title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
transfer: Self-explanation by the model is not a reliable view of its true reason. Shuffle option order across calls and compare, rather than trusting the stated reasoning.

claim: Reasoning-model CoTs reveal a used hint often below 20% of the time; outcome RL raises faithfulness only partway, and reward hacking does not raise verbalization.
quote: the reveal rate is often below 20%
authors: Chen, Benton, Radhakrishnan, Uesato, et al.
title: Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think
transfer: Monitoring the model's own stated reasoning (self-report) is weak; use external signals such as agreement and checks.

claim: LLM verbalized confidence is overconfident; sample consistency helps; white-box vs black-box gap is small (AUROC 0.522 vs 0.605 in the cited case); all methods struggle on professional-knowledge tasks.
quote: LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident.
authors: Xiong, Hu, Lu, Li, Fu, He, Hooi
title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
transfer: Use sample agreement, not stated confidence, as the feeling-of-rightness signal; AUROC near 0.6 means it is a weak gate, not a verdict.

claim: LLM evaluators favor their own outputs, and self-recognition strength tracks the bias (linear after fine-tuning), so self-judgment is biased.
authors: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng
title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
transfer: Judge candidates in a separate call that hides authorship, or with a program check.

claim: Monitoring and control dissociate in 20 LLMs: retrospective monitoring and prospective regulation correlate r=.17 with a wide CI; accuracy rank and metacognitive sensitivity rank are largely inverted. Single author, small number of models, partly exploratory.
authors: Cacioli
title: The Metacognitive Monitoring Battery: A Cross-Domain Benchmark for LLM Self-Monitoring
venue: arXiv 2604.15702 v2 (preprint, submitted to NeurIPS 2026 E&D)
transfer: Do not assume a stronger model monitors better; measure the router signal on our own model per suite.

claim: The 2026 metacognitive harness (FOK before, JOL after each attempt) lifts pooled accuracy 48.3 to 56.9 on Sonnet-4.6, but the page reports no token, latency or call counts, accuracy is pooled across benchmarks, and it is one version of a preprint. Gain net of cost is unknown.
authors: Cao, Wang, Qin, Zhang, Xie
title: LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
transfer: Replicate only with an equal-token best-of-N arm before adopting FOK/JOL steps.

claim: Null result against the warmth-signal idea: warmth ratings did not differ between insight and noninsight magic-trick solutions (p=.429), contrary to Metcalfe and Wiebe 1987; authors suggest few ratings per trial may explain it. 51 students, 971 trials.
authors: Hedne, Norman, Metcalfe
title: Intuitive Feelings of Warmth and Confidence in Insight and Noninsight Problem Solving of Magic Tricks
transfer: Do not gate on a self-rated 'getting close' signal; use observable progress (check output change).

claim: Productive failure meta-analysis covers 53 studies and 166 comparisons; the PF effect has mostly been examined and replicated in STEM, mainly mathematics, and evidence is lacking on whether it depends on domain structuredness (the second point is from a different Springer paper whose authors I did not identify).
authors: Sinha and Kapur
title: When problem solving followed by instruction works: evidence for productive failure
transfer: Do not generalize productive failure to open or ill-structured agent tasks without a test; the domain boundary is unproven. Publisher pages were blocked for me, so figures come from a search snippet.

claim: A critic argues the productive failure control (flipped order, odd control tasks) lacks ecological validity and that his own multi-problem study favored explicit teaching first. This is an opinion post by one researcher with no quantitative reanalysis; the 'eccentricities' of the meta-analysis are not specified.
quote: unlike anything you are likely to see in an explicit teaching classroom
authors: Ashman
title: Is productive struggle ethical?
transfer: Treat productive failure for the agent (try first, then show lesson) as a hypothesis to test against lesson-first at equal tokens, not a given.
